bill.title: A joint resolution proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: Organizations that spend money to influence elections would face new potential restrictions on their expenditures and fundraising.
The amendment would create new constitutional authority to regulate campaign finance, directly affecting election law practice and lobbying activity.
Limits on campaign spending could affect demand for political advertising across broadcast, digital, and print media platforms.
The amendment's authorization to distinguish between natural persons and corporations could affect how financial institutions participate in election-related spending.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment that would allow Congress and state governments to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit lawmakers to treat corporations and other legal entities differently from individual people, including by prohibiting those entities from spending money on elections. The amendment would require ratification by three-fourths of the states to take effect.

bill.title: A joint resolution to direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against the Islamic Republic of Iran that have not been authorized by Congress.
bill.latestActionText: Motion to discharge Senate Committee on Foreign Relations rejected by Yea-Nay Vote. 47 - 53. Record Vote Number: 46. (consideration: CR S796)

industries.rationale: The resolution would directly affect deployment decisions and operational tempo for defense contractors supporting military operations in or near Iran.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would require the President to withdraw U.S. military forces from any hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress has formally declared war or passed specific authorization for such military action. The measure includes an exception allowing the United States to defend itself and its personnel or facilities abroad if attacked. It does not authorize new military operations but instead seeks to limit existing or future ones that lack explicit congressional approval.

bill.title: A joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared to impose duties on articles imported from Canada.
subjects: Presidents and presidential powers, Vice Presidents

industries.rationale: The resolution directly affects the 10% tariff on Canadian energy and energy resources.
The 25% tariff on most Canadian imports affects manufacturers who source materials, components, or finished goods from Canada.
Retailers importing consumer goods from Canada face the 25% tariff that this resolution would eliminate.
Agricultural products and food imports from Canada are subject to the 25% tariff.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would end the national emergency that President Trump declared on February 1, 2025, which imposed a 25% tariff on most goods imported from Canada and a 10% tariff on Canadian energy imports. Terminating the emergency would remove the legal basis for these additional duties on Canadian products.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys imported goods, and people who make goods here.

bill.title: A joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared with respect to energy.
bill.latestActionText: Failed of passage in Senate by Yea-Nay Vote. 47 - 52. Record Vote Number: 95. (consideration: CR S1364, S1367-1390)

industries.rationale: The emergency declaration explicitly directs expedited approval of oil, gas, and coal development and infrastructure; terminating it would remove those fast-track authorities.
The emergency order covers renewable resources and energy storage; ending it would affect expedited permitting for solar, wind, and grid projects.
The emergency declaration includes critical minerals and uranium extraction; termination would remove expedited development authorities for these materials.
The emergency order addresses energy infrastructure and supply adequacy; utilities would lose access to expedited permitting for transmission and generation projects.
The emergency invokes military construction authority and expedited infrastructure completion; terminating it would affect contractors working on energy-related projects.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would end the national energy emergency that the President declared in January 2025. That emergency declaration directed federal agencies to speed up approvals for energy projects—including oil, gas, coal, renewables, and infrastructure like pipelines—and gave the Defense Department authority to use emergency construction powers to address energy supply vulnerabilities. Terminating the emergency would remove those expedited authorities and return permitting and development processes to their standard procedures.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys fuel or heats a home. People who live near a mine, and people who work in one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
